thread.title_full: The common household ingredient that causes 1.9million deaths every year - as Aussies are warned to lower their intake

author: Elijah
title: The common household ingredient that causes 1.9million deaths every year - as Aussies are warned to lower their intake
text:
By Xiaoyue (Luna) Professor of Scientist Xu, Population Health School, Unsw Sydney and Bruce Neal Executive Director, George Institute Australia, George Institute for Global Health
This week, the World Health Organization published new guidelines that recommend that people change the regular salt they use at home for substitutes containing less sodium.
But what exactly are these salt alternatives? And why is WHO recommends this? Let’s take a look.
A new solution to an old problem
The advice to eat less salt (sodium chloride) is not new. It has been part of the international and Australian guidelines for decades. This is because the evidence clearly shows that sodium in salt can damage our health when we eat too much.
Excess sodium increases the risk of high blood pressure, affecting millions of Australians (around one in three adults). High blood pressure (hypertension) in turn increases the risk of heart disease, stroke and kidney disease, among other conditions.
WHO estimates 1.9 million deaths worldwide every year can be attributed to eating too much salt.
WHO recommends consuming no more than 2 g of sodium daily. However, people eat on average more than double this, about 4.3ga day.
In 2013, WHO Member States promised to reduce the population’s sodium intake by 30 percent by 2025. But cutting salt intake has proven to be very difficult. Most countries, including Australia, will not meet WHO’s objective to reduce sodium intake by 2025. WHO has established the same objective by 2030.
There have been few progress in efforts to reduce sodium intake.
The difficulty is that eating less salt means accepting a less salty flavor. It also requires changes in established ways to prepare food. This has shown too much to ask people to make food at home and too much for the food industry.
Enter salt enriched with potassium
The main substitute for low sodium salt is called salt enriched with potassium. This is salt where part of the sodium chloride has been replaced by potassium chloride.
Potassium is an essential mineral that plays a key role in all body functions. The high potassium content of fresh fruits and vegetables is one of the main reasons why they are so good for you. While people eat more sodium than they should, many do not get enough potassium.
WHO recommends a daily potassium intake of 3.5 g, but in general, people in most countries consume significantly less than this.
Salt enriched with potassium benefits our health by reducing the amount of sodium we consume and increasing the amount of potassium in our diets. Both help reduce blood pressure.
It has been shown that changing regular salt due to salt enriched with potassium reduces the risk of heart disease, stroke and premature death in large trials worldwide.
Modeling studies have projected that switches throughout the population to the use of salt enriched with potassium would avoid hundreds of thousands of deaths from cardiovascular disease (such as heart attack and stroke) every year in China and India.
The key advantage of changing instead of cutting salt intake is that salt enriched with potassium can be used as a direct exchange one by one for regular salt. It looks the same, it works for seasoning and in recipes, and most people do not notice any important difference in taste.
Excess sodium intake increases high blood pressure risk, which can cause a variety of health problems
In the largest salt trial with potassium to date, more than 90% of people still used the product after five years.
Make change: some challenges
If it is completely implemented, this could be one of the most consistent advice you have provided.
Millions of blows and heart attacks could be avoided around the world every year with a simple change to the way we prepare food. But there are some obstacles to overcome before reaching this point.
First, it will be important to balance the benefits and risks. For example, people with advanced kidney disease do not handle potassium well, so these products are not suitable for them. This is just a small proportion of the population, but we must ensure that salt products with potassium are labeled with appropriate warnings.
A key challenge will be to make salt enriched with potassium more affordable and accessible. Potassium chloride is more expensive to produce than sodium chloride, and currently, salt enriched with potassium is sold mainly as a niche health product at a premium price.
If you are looking for it, salt substitutes can also be called low sodium salt, potassium salt, cardiac salt, mineral salt or salt reduced salt.
A review published in 2021 found low sodium salts were marketed in just 47 countries, mostly high income. Prices varied from the same as regular salt to almost 15 times more.
An expanded supply chain will be needed that produces much more food degree potassium chloride to allow the broader availability of the product. And we will need to see salt enriched with potassium on the shelves next to regular salt, so it is easy to find for people.
In countries such as Australia, about 80% of the salt we eat comes from processed foods
In countries such as Australia, about 80% of the salt we eat comes from processed foods. The WHO guideline falls short by not explicitly prioritizing a salt switch used in food manufacturing.
The interested parties that work with the government to encourage the absorption of the food industry will be essential to maximize health benefits.
